articles.title: A 60-year-old theory about ants, bees and wasps may be wrong
articles.summary: Scientists have long thought an unusual genetic system helped ants, bees, and wasps evolve their extraordinary social colonies. A massive new analysis suggests that genetics alone can’t explain it—and the real secret may lie in other traits unique to these insects.
articles.content:
For more than six decades, evolutionary biologists have debated whether an unusual genetic system shared by ants, bees and wasps helped drive one of nature's most sophisticated forms of social organization: eusociality. In eusocial colonies, reproduction is divided between queens and workers, creating highly cooperative societies with specialized roles.

New research from Arizona State University now suggests that genetics alone may not explain how these complex societies evolved.

Published in Current Biology, the study found that eusociality does seem to arise more often among insects with a haplodiploid genetic system. However, nearly all of that pattern can be traced to one particular group: the aculeate Hymenoptera, which includes stinging wasps, bees and ants. When insects are considered more broadly, haplodiploidy alone does not reliably predict whether eusociality will evolve.

The results suggest that the repeated emergence of complex insect societies may depend more on biological traits specific to certain evolutionary groups than on the way chromosomes are inherited.

"People have been discussing this hypothesis for about 60 years," said Sachin Suresh, a PhD student in the School of Life Sciences at Arizona State University and lead author of the study. "There were many theoretical predictions, but formal comparative tests across insects have been surprisingly rare."

Why Eusocial Insects Are So Unusual

Eusociality is considered one of the most advanced forms of social organization in the natural world. Species that live this way form colonies containing overlapping generations, cooperate in raising young and divide reproductive responsibilities. Only one individual or a small number of individuals reproduce, while the others serve as workers.

All ants are eusocial, along with honey bees and some wasps. By contrast, eusociality has appeared only rarely in other insect groups, including termites, thrips, aphids and a small number of beetles.

For many years, scientists have focused on haplodiploidy as a possible explanation for why this lifestyle evolved so often in ants, bees and wasps. Under this genetic system, females develop from fertilized eggs and possess two sets of chromosomes, while males develop from unfertilized eggs and have only one set.

This arrangement can make sisters more closely related to one another than they are to their own offspring. Evolutionary theory therefore proposed that females might sometimes gain a greater evolutionary advantage by helping raise their sisters than by producing offspring of their own.

The idea became highly influential in evolutionary biology and eventually appeared widely in biology textbooks. Despite its importance, however, the hypothesis had rarely been evaluated using large empirical datasets spanning a broad range of insects.

Testing a 60 Year Old Evolutionary Idea

To put the hypothesis to a large scale test, Suresh and senior author Timothy Linksvayer assembled information on social behavior and genetics from tens of thousands of insect species. They then placed those characteristics onto two of the largest available species level insect family trees.

Using phylogenetic comparative methods, the researchers estimated how frequently eusociality evolved among insects with different genetic systems.

Initially, the findings appeared to support the traditional explanation. Eusociality seemed to emerge more frequently among haplodiploid insects.

A deeper examination, however, produced a very different picture. Nearly the entire statistical signal was coming from a single branch of the insect family tree.

"When we formally tested it, we found there is no real association between the genetic determination system and eusociality," Suresh said. "It has more to do with environmental factors and the life-history traits of insects."

After accounting for the unusual evolutionary history of the aculeate Hymenoptera, the researchers found that haplodiploid insects outside that group developed eusociality at rates similar to those seen in diploid insects.

Nearly 69,000 Species Reveal a Different Pattern

The findings also help bring together recent research that has raised doubts about how important haplodiploidy really is to the evolution of complex insect societies.

By examining nearly 69,000 insect species representing a wide range of insect diversity, the Arizona State University team found that the apparent connection between haplodiploidy and eusociality is largely the result of evolutionary history within particular lineages. It does not appear to represent a universal biological rule.

That shifts attention toward other characteristics that may have helped ants, bees and wasps repeatedly evolve highly cooperative colonies.

Features such as stingers, specialized nesting behaviors and other biological traits may have created conditions that made cooperation more advantageous and helped sophisticated insect societies emerge again and again.

The research represents one of the most comprehensive empirical tests yet of a foundational idea in evolutionary biology. It also highlights the value of using large comparative datasets to revisit theories that have remained influential for decades.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough that challenges a 60-year-old evolutionary biology theory about eusociality in insects. This new research, based on a large dataset of nearly 69,000 insect species, shifts understanding of how complex social behaviors evolved, highlighting the importance of traits beyond genetics. The findings have broad implications for evolutionary biology and demonstrate the power of large-scale data analysis in revising long-standing scientific ideas.
articles.personality_title: New study challenges 60-year-old idea about insect social behavior
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long believed that a special genetic system called haplodiploidy helped ants, bees, and wasps develop their complex social colonies. In these colonies, only some insects reproduce while others work together to support them.

**What happened** – Researchers at Arizona State University studied nearly 69,000 insect species to test this idea. They found that while eusocial behavior (living in highly cooperative groups) is common in insects with haplodiploid genetics, this pattern mainly comes from one group: stinging wasps, bees, and ants. Outside this group, genetics alone does not explain eusociality.

**Impact** – This research shows that the old theory, which has been accepted for 60 years, may not fully explain why these insects form social colonies. Instead, other traits like having stingers or specific nesting habits might be more important in helping these insects work together. This changes how scientists think about the evolution of social behavior in insects.

**What's next step** – Scientists will now look more closely at other biological traits and environmental factors that may influence social living in insects. This could lead to new discoveries about how cooperation evolved in nature.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A large new study reveals that insect social behavior depends more on unique traits than on genetics alone, challenging a long-held scientific idea.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle étude remet en cause une idée vieille de 60 ans sur le comportement social des insectes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques pensaient depuis longtemps qu’un système génétique spécial appelé haplodiploïdie aidait les fourmis, les abeilles et les guêpes à développer leurs colonies sociales complexes. Dans ces colonies, seuls certains individus se reproduisent tandis que les autres travaillent ensemble pour les soutenir.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université d’État de l’Arizona ont étudié près de 69 000 espèces d’insectes pour tester cette idée. Ils ont découvert que, bien que le comportement eusocial (vivre en groupes très coopératifs) soit fréquent chez les insectes haplodiploïdes, ce schéma vient surtout d’un groupe : les guêpes piqueuses, les abeilles et les fourmis. En dehors de ce groupe, la génétique seule n’explique pas l’eusocialité.

**Impact** – Cette recherche montre que la vieille théorie, acceptée depuis 60 ans, n’explique pas complètement pourquoi ces insectes forment des colonies sociales. D’autres traits, comme avoir un dard ou des habitudes de nidification spécifiques, pourraient être plus importants pour aider ces insectes à coopérer. Cela change la façon dont les scientifiques comprennent l’évolution du comportement social chez les insectes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont maintenant étudier de plus près d’autres traits biologiques et facteurs environnementaux qui pourraient influencer la vie sociale des insectes. Cela pourrait conduire à de nouvelles découvertes sur l’évolution de la coopération dans la nature.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une grande étude révèle que le comportement social des insectes dépend davantage de traits uniques que de la génétique seule, remettant en question une idée scientifique ancienne.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo estudio desafía una idea de 60 años sobre el comportamiento social de los insectos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos creyeron que un sistema genético especial llamado haplodiploidía ayudó a las hormigas, abejas y avispas a desarrollar sus complejas colonias sociales. En estas colonias, solo algunos insectos se reproducen mientras otros trabajan juntos para apoyarlos.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad Estatal de Arizona estudiaron cerca de 69,000 especies de insectos para probar esta idea. Encontraron que, aunque el comportamiento eusocial (vivir en grupos muy cooperativos) es común en insectos con genética haplodiploide, este patrón proviene principalmente de un grupo: las avispas con aguijón, abejas y hormigas. Fuera de este grupo, la genética por sí sola no explica la eusocialidad.

**Impacto** – Esta investigación muestra que la antigua teoría, aceptada durante 60 años, no explica completamente por qué estos insectos forman colonias sociales. En cambio, otros rasgos como tener aguijones o hábitos de anidación específicos podrían ser más importantes para ayudar a estos insectos a cooperar. Esto cambia la forma en que los científicos piensan sobre la evolución del comportamiento social en los insectos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos ahora examinarán más de cerca otros rasgos biológicos y factores ambientales que pueden influir en la vida social de los insectos. Esto podría llevar a nuevos descubrimientos sobre cómo evolucionó la cooperación en la naturaleza.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un gran estudio revela que el comportamiento social de los insectos depende más de rasgos únicos que solo de la genética, desafiando una idea científica muy antigua.
